reasons.rubric: Boolean validity-window predicate from a hospital issuer is simple, but frequency is episodic and nursing homes have no mandate to accept digital proof, so a good-not-strong fit.
reasons.validity: Visitor screening at care homes during outbreaks is real and hospitals could sign a test-result window, but the facility's own window rule may differ from the signed N days.
reasons.coherence: Predicate, issuer and verifier line up well, though 'no active restriction' versus 'negative test' are subtly different claims.
reasons.novelty: Health-status gating of access is not on the known list, though it is a familiar proof-of-status pattern.
reasons.provenance: The selective-disclosure borrowing is generic and the holder-binding borrowing is partly real, but the idea reads much the same without either.
reasons.retention_law: Nursing homes have no evident duty to keep the lab report, and infection-control logs may need only a pass/fail record.
reasons.linkability: A short-lived attestation shown at a front desk is low-risk, though repeated presentations of the same signed token could be correlated.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Hospitals and clinics have little incentive or tooling to issue machine-verifiable negative-test attestations to non-patients' visitors.
reasons.no_wallet: Elderly relatives and foreign caregivers are unlikely to hold a compatible wallet, and the front desk has no verifier.

reasons.rubric: Multi-source same-person match across two issuers plus a likely occupational-health requirement for fuller data makes this a design-heavy, low-frequency case.
reasons.validity: Clinical placements do require vaccination and enrolment checks, but the hospital probably needs specific vaccine details, so the matching predicate alone is insufficient.
reasons.coherence: The match proof covers only the eligibility gate while the idea concedes fuller disclosure is still needed, which undercuts the stated benefit.
reasons.novelty: Student placement onboarding is a new moment, loosely near the degree and licence cases but with a cross-issuer binding.
reasons.provenance: The unlinkable-redemption and law-enforcement-exception borrowings are decorative and the second is unrelated to occupational health.
reasons.retention_law: Hospitals have occupational-health obligations and may be required to keep vaccination records, which erodes the benefit.
reasons.linkability: Cross-issuer same-person matching without revealing ID needs a shared binding key, which is feasible but adds a linkage point.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: No health-authority or university issuer currently signs these claims, and aligning two issuers is hard.
reasons.no_wallet: Students and university or hospital HR can plausibly adopt a wallet, so this is a minor barrier.

reasons.rubric: A non-membership predicate is simple, but it needs a government-signed absence attestation that does not exist and the dealer still needs identity, so it is only possible.
reasons.validity: Dealers do worry about seized or encumbered vehicles, but that is a property of the vehicle rather than the seller, and the description conflates exit restrictions with seizure.
reasons.coherence: The title mentions exit restriction but the predicate is about vehicle seizure, and the buyer or seller roles are blurred.
reasons.novelty: Used-car transfer and encumbrance is a moment not touched by the known list, though ID-copy over-collection resembles known cases.
reasons.provenance: The ID-copy over-collection pattern is real but the idea would read the same without citing it, so the borrowing is decorative.
reasons.retention_law: Vehicle transfer paperwork likely requires the dealer to hold identity documents, so the legal position is uncertain.
reasons.linkability: A one-time signed non-membership statement tied to a plate is low-linkability, but the legal name is revealed anyway.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: It requires the highways authority and the judiciary to jointly publish signed absence attestations, which is a large coordination ask.
reasons.no_wallet: Dealers could verify through a web tool, and sellers are mostly adults with phones, so wallet access is a moderate barrier.

reasons.rubric: A simple current-standing boolean with a plausible employer issuer and daily frequency, but a fragmented platform ecosystem and independent-contractor status reduce it to a good fit.
reasons.validity: Site access control for couriers is a real daily moment and current standing is nearly sufficient, though sites often want a name or plate for incident tracing.
reasons.coherence: Predicate, issuer, revocation and verifier fit together tightly, and the stale-card benefit is a real gain.
reasons.novelty: Gig-worker site access is not on the known list and involves a new issuer type.
reasons.provenance: Borrowings are empty, so provenance does not apply.
reasons.retention_law: Nothing evident requires the gatekeeper to retain the ID, and incident tracing is a policy preference rather than a known legal duty.
reasons.linkability: Daily repeat entries risk correlation unless proofs are unlinkable, but the verifier is local and the stakes are low.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Platforms have an incentive to control access and revoke quickly, but may resist employer-style attestations because of contractor status.
reasons.no_wallet: Couriers carry smartphones and are used to platform apps, though many separate security gates lack verifier tooling.

reasons.rubric: The predicate combines a sum threshold and a count over transactions, which is a more complex range proof, and the verifier has commercial reasons to see more and holds power over the worker.
reasons.validity: Remittance regularity as a signal for lenders is plausible, but the stated moment is muddled and the broker's real need is probably wage and debt information.
reasons.coherence: The verifier list mixes a broker, a foreign lender and a visa service with different needs, and the idea itself admits the verifier may simply refuse the proof.
reasons.novelty: Migrant-worker remittance proof is a moment nobody on the known list touches.
reasons.provenance: The borrowed minimum-necessary framing is generic and the idea reads the same without it, and the HIPAA excerpt is from an unrelated domain.
reasons.retention_law: Banks must retain transaction records, but the verifier is a broker or lender with no evident duty to keep the full statements.
reasons.linkability: Aggregate proofs over six months of transfers are linkable to the worker's bank, but the verifier would learn little else.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Banks would have to sign aggregate proofs for a niche population with little commercial return, which is unlikely without regulation.
reasons.no_wallet: Migrant workers have smartphones, but a home-country verifier needs compatible tooling, and bargaining power makes adoption unlikely.

reasons.rubric: Geographic-roll membership is a simple predicate, but issuers are fragmented across utilities and the verifier may legally need the registered address, so it needs design.
reasons.validity: Schools asking for bills as address proof is real, but the tenant often is not the account holder and household registration is typically the actual rule, so sufficiency is doubtful.
reasons.coherence: The scenario is partly confused because a catchment test normally runs on the household register rather than a utility roll, and it admits the account holder may differ from the tenant.
reasons.novelty: It sits close to the known address-matches-roll utility subsidy case and the renting-address case, only moving to a school verifier.
reasons.provenance: The borrowings are descriptions of over-collection that the idea would state anyway, so they are decorative.
reasons.retention_law: Schools probably must keep enrolment evidence and may need the household registration address regardless, which is uncertain in detail.
reasons.linkability: A coarse district membership claim has low linkability if the account identifier is not exposed.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Taiwan Water Corporation and Taipower have no mandate or incentive to sign geographic roll membership for third-party use.
reasons.no_wallet: Parents have phones, but school admin desks lack verifier tooling.

reasons.rubric: A simple boolean with an existing employer issuer and daily frequency, but the stakes are tiny and identity is often needed for payroll deduction, so it is a good but marginal fit.
reasons.validity: Staff-rate checks at concessions are real, and active status suffices for cash or point-of-sale discounts, but payroll-linked discounts need identity.
reasons.coherence: The parts fit well, and the idea honestly limits the benefit to non-payroll discounts.
reasons.novelty: It is a new issuer type and moment, though the predicate is close to the known proof-of-employment pattern.
reasons.provenance: Unlinkable redemption is a real driver of the privacy benefit here because it prevents a meal and parking visit log, but the cited source is generic.
reasons.retention_law: No law evidently requires concessionaires to log staff identity for a meal discount.
reasons.linkability: Repeated daily use makes linkability the central concern, and it only holds if proofs are truly unlinkable.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Hospitals and contractors have little reason to build daily-refresh credential issuance for a cafeteria discount.
reasons.no_wallet: Cashiers and parking systems would need new verifier tooling and cleaners may have limited wallet adoption.

reasons.rubric: A one-person-one-vote nullifier is a uniqueness proof like the known Sybil case, but the issuer is a telco that does not prove residence, and the vote rules need weights, so it needs design.
reasons.validity: Community polls are real, but a telco subscriber is not a resident or owner, and condominium voting is weighted by ownership, so the predicate is insufficient.
reasons.coherence: The idea itself says the credential does not prove residence and the voting rules differ, so the issuer and predicate do not match the decision.
reasons.novelty: It is largely a reuse of the known one-person-one-account nullifier predicate on a new moment.
reasons.provenance: Borrowings are empty, so provenance does not apply.
reasons.retention_law: A committee may need records of who voted for legitimacy of weighted votes, which is uncertain under condominium rules.
reasons.linkability: A per-poll nullifier is designed for this purpose and avoids linking votes to subscribers.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Mobile carriers have little reason to sign uniqueness credentials for community polls.
reasons.no_wallet: Residents of all ages must use it, committees run LINE polls, and no wallet or verifier tooling exists in that setting.
